title: Transferable Multiform Attack for Cross-Modal Person Re-Identification
claim: Prior attacks optimize one perturbation on fixed source pairs and transfer poorly; ours adds a sparse evolutionary stage for broad transfer.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, top-to-bottom flow, cyclic arrows, ✗/✓ outcome row at bottom
description: Two side-by-side panels. Panel (a), 'Traditional Cross-Modality Attack', and panel (b), 'Unified Multiform Attack', both start with the same row of pedestrian image stacks from two modalities, M1 (RGB) and M2 (grayscale/infrared), each with negative and positive samples (Cn, Cp). A large blue arrow leads down to a push/pull embedding diagram. In (a) this is blue and orange blobs. In (b) it is contour-line fields. Cyclic Optimize and Attack arrows loop through a single noise perturbation δ. At the bottom, a row of retrieval results across modalities M1 to M4 is marked with red ✗ and green ✓, and the caption reads 'Poor Transferability'. Panel (b) adds a dashed box combining the universal perturbation δ with a sparse perturbation η, plus an orange Evaluation and Attack loop. Brackets on the right label 'Gradient-based Learning of δ' and 'Evolutionary Search of η'. All four results are ✗, and the caption reads 'Unified and Highly Transferable'. The eye goes first to the bold red captions and the contrasting ✗/✓ rows.
caption: Comparison between traditional gradient-based cross-modal attacks and the proposed MA. Conventional methods optimize perturbations over fixed source modality pairs, which may cause attacks to overfit source-pair-specific embedding relationships and limit their transferability to unseen modalities. MA couples Mahalanobis-guided universal perturbation learning with structure-aware sparse evolutionary refinement, shifting the optimization focus from source-pair effectiveness toward cross-modal transferability.
abstract: Cross-modal person re-identification (ReID) adversarial attacks face a transferability challenge: existing methods may exhibit source-pair overfitting, where learned perturbations become overly dependent on the feature statistics of the source modality pair, thereby limiting their transferability under heterogeneous domain shifts. We argue that a key challenge is reducing source-pair-specific bias while maintaining attack effectiveness. To address this, we propose Multiform Attack (MA). The framework first learns a universal perturbation via Mahalanobis-guided gradient optimization. Since this perturbation may still retain source-pair-specific bias, the second stage performs sparse refinement through attention-shift-filtered multi-objective evolutionary search, leveraging heterogeneous source distributions in transfer settings. By separating universal perturbation learning from sparse evolutionary refinement, MA aims to reduce reliance on source-pair-specific patterns and improve transferability to unseen domains. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong attack effectiveness on cross-modal ReID benchmarks and improved transferability in the evaluated held-out-domain settings, with additional evaluations across model architectures.
